chapter.name: Shaping of the Earth's Surface
chapter.blurb: Earth's interior and plate tectonics, earthquakes and volcanoes, weathering and erosion, landforms made by rivers, waves, glaciers, wind and groundwater, and landform disasters.

scope_in.item: Layers of the Earth, lithosphere, asthenosphere, tectonic plates and convection currents
Plate boundaries, earthquakes, volcanoes and the Ring of Fire; earthquake risk in India
Weathering, erosion, agents of gradation and soil conservation practices
River landforms: waterfalls, meanders and deltas and their use
Landforms of waves, glaciers, wind and underground water and their use to humans
Landslides, avalanches, GLOFs and dust storms: causes and mitigation

scope_out.item: Detailed study of oceans, waves and currents
scope_out.reason: The text says this comes in Part 2

scope_out.item: Seismology, magnitude scales and prediction methods
Rock cycle and types of rocks

concepts.name: The interior of the Earth and plate tectonics
concepts.description: The layers of the Earth, the lithosphere and asthenosphere, tectonic plates and the convection currents that move them.
concepts.idea: The outer layer of the Earth is broken into plates that move slowly over a semi-molten layer beneath them.
concepts.rule: Earth has crust, mantle and core. The crust with the upper mantle forms the lithosphere, broken into tectonic plates. The asthenosphere is semi-molten and lets plates move. Plates move a few centimetres a year, driven by convection currents in the mantle.
concepts.example: Crust is 30-40 km thick under continents and 5-7 km under oceans; the mantle is about 2900 km thick.

questions.q: The three main layers of the Earth are
questions.a: crust, mantle and core

questions.q: The theory that explains the movement of the Earth's crust in broken pieces is called
questions.a: plate tectonics

questions.q: The crust together with the upper part of the mantle forms the ____.
questions.a: lithosphere

questions.q: The semi-molten layer below the lithosphere is the
questions.a: asthenosphere

questions.q: Tectonic plates move
questions.a: very slowly, a few centimetres a year
o: very slowly, a few centimetres a year

questions.q: The three main types of tectonic plates are
questions.a: continental, oceanic and mixed

questions.q: The movement of tectonic plates is caused by
questions.a: convection currents in the mantle

questions.q: The innermost layer of the Earth is
questions.a: the core

questions.q: Explain how convection currents move tectonic plates.
questions.a: Heat from the core makes molten material in the mantle rise while cooler material sinks. This continuous movement creates convection currents that push and pull the plates in different directions.
s: Hot material rises and cooler material sinks
This pushes and pulls the plates

questions.q: The crust under the oceans is about
questions.a: 5-7 km thick

questions.q: The crust under the continents is about ____ km thick (give the range, for example 30-40).
Which of these is a major tectonic plate?
questions.a: Indo-Australian Plate

questions.q: Name two major tectonic plates.
questions.a: For example the Pacific Plate and the African Plate (others: Eurasian, North American, South American, Indo-Australian, Antarctic).

questions.q: Distinguish continental, oceanic and mixed plates.
questions.a: Continental plates carry continents, oceanic plates carry ocean floors and mixed plates carry both continents and oceans.

questions.q: Describe the interior of the Earth from the surface to the centre.
questions.a: The crust is the outer layer on which we live (about 5 km under oceans and 30 km under continents). Below it is the thick, hot mantle (about 2900 km). At the centre is the core, with a fluid outer core of iron and nickel (about 2200 km) and a solid, hot inner core (about 1250 km).

questions.q: Plates can move because below the lithosphere lies
questions.a: a semi-molten asthenosphere

questions.q: Why is the theory of plate tectonics important?
questions.a: It explains how the Earth's surface changes and the origin of landforms and natural disasters, and helps identify earthquake and volcano-prone regions and manage disasters.
s: Helps identify prone regions and manage disasters

questions.q: Explain the relation between the lithosphere, the asthenosphere and tectonic plates.
questions.a: The lithosphere is the rigid outer layer made of the crust and upper mantle. It is broken into tectonic plates. Below it the asthenosphere is semi-molten, which allows the plates to move over it.
s: Says it is broken into plates
Says the semi-molten asthenosphere lets plates move

questions.q: Ravi says the Earth's outer layer is a single unbroken piece. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. The outermost layer is broken into several large and small tectonic plates that move slowly.
s: Says it is broken into plates

questions.q: Describe a simple labelled diagram of the Earth's layers, from outside to inside.
questions.a: Draw circles and label the crust (outermost), the mantle, the outer core and the inner core at the centre, marking the lithosphere and asthenosphere, with approximate thicknesses.

concepts.name: Plate boundaries, earthquakes and volcanoes
concepts.description: The three types of plate boundaries and the earthquakes, volcanoes and mountains they produce, the Ring of Fire and earthquake risk in India.
concepts.idea: Most earthquakes and volcanoes occur where plates meet; the type of boundary decides what forms.
concepts.rule: Convergent: plates move together (fold mountains like the Himalaya; oceanic plate sinks under a continental plate causing volcanoes and earthquakes). Divergent: plates move apart and new crust forms (Mid-Atlantic Ridge). Transform: plates slide past (San Andreas Fault) causing earthquakes.
concepts.example: Most earthquakes and volcanoes occur around the Pacific Ocean, the Ring of Fire.

questions.q: The three main types of plate boundaries are
questions.a: convergent, divergent and transform

questions.q: The Himalaya were formed by the collision of
questions.a: continental plates

questions.q: Most earthquakes and volcanoes occur around the Pacific Ocean in the Ring of ____.
questions.a: Fire

questions.q: The Mid-Atlantic Ridge is an example of a
questions.a: divergent boundary

questions.q: At a divergent boundary
questions.a: plates move away and magma rises to form new crust
o: plates move away and magma rises to form new crust
plates slide past without changing crust

questions.q: At a transform boundary plates
questions.a: slide past each other and mainly cause earthquakes
o: slide past each other and mainly cause earthquakes

questions.q: When an oceanic plate meets a continental plate
questions.a: the oceanic plate sinks below, causing volcanic activity and earthquakes
o: the oceanic plate sinks below, causing volcanic activity and earthquakes
the continental plate sinks into the ocean floor

questions.q: Most earthquakes and volcanoes occur
questions.a: along plate boundaries
o: only in the centre of plates

questions.q: Why does the Pacific Ocean region, the Ring of Fire, have many earthquakes and volcanoes?
questions.a: It lies along boundaries of several plates. Most earthquakes and volcanoes occur along plate boundaries where plates collide, separate or slide past each other.
s: Says it lies along plate boundaries
Says earthquakes and volcanoes occur there

questions.q: In early times an earthquake was called
questions.a: bhukampa

questions.q: Bhukampa means the ____ of the Earth.
questions.a: shaking

questions.q: In the Brihatsamhita Varahamihira noted that signs of an earthquake could include
questions.a: changes in wind, rain, clouds, animal behaviour and planetary alignments
o: changes in wind, rain, clouds, animal behaviour and planetary alignments

questions.q: State what happens at (i) a convergent boundary and (ii) a divergent boundary.
questions.a: (i) Plates move towards each other, forming fold mountains or causing volcanoes and earthquakes. (ii) Plates move apart and magma rises to form new crust, creating features such as mid-ocean ridges.

questions.q: What is special about the mud volcano at Baratang Island?
questions.a: It is India's only mud volcano, in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands. Unlike fiery volcanoes, mud bubbles out because of natural underground gases and pressure.
s: India's only mud volcano in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands
Mud bubbles out due to gases and pressure

questions.q: Explain the two kinds of convergent boundary.
questions.a: When two continental plates collide they form fold mountains, such as the Himalaya. When an oceanic plate collides with a continental plate, the oceanic plate sinks beneath the continental plate, leading to volcanic activity and earthquakes.
s: Oceanic plate sinks, giving volcanoes and earthquakes

questions.q: A large earthquake in a densely populated country like India can cause
questions.a: severe damage to life and environment
o: severe damage to life and environment

questions.q: What does the 2001 Gujarat earthquake show about earthquakes in India?
questions.a: India has had major earthquakes that caused thousands of deaths and extensive damage, so earthquakes are a real risk in its densely populated regions.
s: Says India has experienced major earthquakes
Says they caused loss of life and damage

questions.q: Compare the three types of plate boundaries: how plates move, what is formed and one example.
questions.a: Convergent: plates move together, fold mountains, volcanoes and earthquakes, for example the Himalaya. Divergent: plates move apart, new crust and mid-ocean ridges, for example the Mid-Atlantic Ridge. Transform: plates slide past, earthquakes, for example the San Andreas Fault.

questions.q: Sam says earthquakes and volcanoes occur at random all over the Earth. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. They mostly occur along plate boundaries, for example around the Pacific Ocean in the Ring of Fire.
s: Says they occur along plate boundaries

questions.q: Comparing a map of plates with a map of earthquakes and volcanoes, what relationship would you point out? Give reasons.
questions.a: The earthquakes and volcanoes cluster along the plate boundaries, especially around the Pacific. This is because the plates collide, separate or slide past there and the crust is disturbed.
s: Says earthquakes and volcanoes lie along plate boundaries
Names the Pacific Ring of Fire
Gives the reason with plate movement

concepts.name: Weathering, erosion and the agents of gradation
concepts.description: Weathering and its types, erosion, how erosion affects livelihoods and soil conservation methods, and the agents that wear down and reshape the surface.
concepts.idea: Weathering breaks rocks; erosion carries the pieces away; together with deposition they reshape the surface.
concepts.rule: Weathering: rocks break down without moving (physical, chemical, biological). Erosion: material is carried away by water, wind, ice or waves. Agents of gradation: running water, glaciers, wind, waves, groundwater. Conservation: contouring, bunding, terracing, check dams.
concepts.example: Plant roots growing into rock cracks and splitting them is biological weathering.

questions.q: Weathering is the process by which
questions.a: rocks break down into smaller pieces without movement
o: rocks break down into smaller pieces without movement
rocks are carried away by rivers

questions.q: The three types of weathering are
questions.a: physical, chemical and biological

questions.q: Erosion involves the ____ of broken material from one place to another.
questions.a: movement

questions.q: The main types of erosion include
questions.a: water, wind, glacial and coastal erosion
o: water, wind, glacial and coastal erosion

questions.q: Plant roots growing into cracks of rocks and splitting them is
questions.a: biological weathering

questions.q: The difference between weathering and erosion is that erosion
questions.a: involves movement of the broken material
o: involves movement of the broken material

questions.q: The main agents of gradation are
questions.a: running water, glaciers, wind, waves and groundwater
o: running water, glaciers, wind, waves and groundwater

questions.q: How does erosion affect farmers?
questions.a: It removes fertile topsoil and lowers crop yields
o: It removes fertile topsoil and lowers crop yields

questions.q: Explain the difference between weathering and erosion.
questions.a: Weathering only breaks rocks into smaller pieces where they are. Erosion wears away the material and carries it from one place to another by water, wind, ice or waves.
s: Weathering is breaking down without movement
Erosion involves carrying the material away

questions.q: Rocks breaking because of temperature changes, frost or wind is
questions.a: physical weathering

questions.q: In chemical weathering, minerals react with water, air or ____.
questions.a: acids

questions.q: The Zabo system of Nagaland is
questions.a: an integrated farming approach using earthen bunds on hillslopes for soil and water conservation
o: an integrated farming approach using earthen bunds on hillslopes for soil and water conservation
a type of dam on the Ganga

questions.q: Explain how erosion affects the occupations of (i) farmers and (ii) people living near rivers and coasts.
questions.a: (i) It removes fertile topsoil and lowers yields. (ii) It can wash away land, houses and roads, causing loss of property.
s: Effect on people near rivers and coasts

questions.q: Give one-line meanings of contouring, bunding and terracing.
questions.a: Contouring: digging trenches along contour lines to hold rainwater. Bunding: earthen embankments along contour lines to slow run-off. Terracing: level or gently sloping steps on a hillside to prevent soil erosion.

questions.q: Describe how different agents of gradation modify landforms.
questions.a: Running water erodes rocks and soil to form valleys and plains. Glaciers scrape and carry material, carving U-shaped valleys. Wind shapes deserts by eroding and depositing sand. Sea waves erode coasts into cliffs, beaches and bays. Groundwater dissolves rocks like limestone, creating caves and sinkholes.

questions.q: Terracing helps because it
questions.a: creates level steps on hillsides to prevent soil erosion
o: creates level steps on hillsides to prevent soil erosion

questions.q: Why did the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation use contouring, bunding, terracing, dams and canals?
questions.a: They were water management and soil conservation techniques that reduced run-off and erosion and stored water.

questions.q: Explain with examples how landforms have shaped human history.
questions.a: Rivers and fertile plains such as the Ganga, Nile, Brahmaputra and Indus gave rise to agricultural societies and cities. Mountains like the Himalayas acted as barriers and protectors and allowed exchange through passes like the Khyber. Deserts such as the Thar limited large settlements but encouraged trade routes like the Silk Route. Coasts and harbours supported trade and cultural contact.
s: Rivers and plains with an example
Mountains or deserts with an example

questions.q: Nita says erosion only destroys landforms. Evaluate.
questions.a: She is wrong. Erosion shapes landforms and can both create and destroy features, for example carving valleys and deltas as well as wearing away land.
s: Says it can create as well as destroy

questions.q: Suggest a plan to protect the land in your locality from erosion, using three ideas from the chapter.
questions.a: Build terraces on slopes, make earthen bunds and contour trenches to slow run-off, build check dams across small streams and keep vegetation cover.
s: Third measure with the reason it helps

concepts.name: Landforms made by rivers: waterfalls, meanders and deltas
concepts.description: How rivers erode, transport and deposit and the landforms of the upper, middle and lower course, and their use by people.
concepts.idea: A river changes as it flows: it erodes strongly in the upper course and deposits in the lower course.
concepts.rule: Upper course: V-shaped valleys, waterfalls, rapids. Middle course: meanders, oxbow lakes, floodplains. Lower course: deltas, levees, alluvial fans. A delta forms where a river deposits sediment at its mouth.
concepts.example: The Sundarbans is a delta; the Grand Anicut (Kallanai) in Tamil Nadu uses a river for irrigation.

questions.q: Rivers shape the land through
questions.a: erosion, transportation and deposition

questions.q: A delta forms
questions.a: at the mouth of a river where it enters a sea, ocean or lake
o: at the mouth of a river where it enters a sea, ocean or lake
at the source of a river

questions.q: A winding bend in the middle or lower course of a river is called a ____.
questions.a: meander

questions.q: V-shaped valleys, waterfalls and rapids are found in the
questions.a: upper course

questions.q: Meanders, oxbow lakes and floodplains are found in the
questions.a: middle course

questions.q: Deltas, levees and alluvial fans are found in the
questions.a: lower course

questions.q: A waterfall forms when
questions.a: a river flows over hard rock while softer rock below is worn away
o: a river flows over hard rock while softer rock below is worn away

questions.q: In a meander the river
questions.a: erodes the outer banks and deposits sediment on the inner banks
o: erodes the outer banks and deposits sediment on the inner banks
deposits on the outer banks and erodes the inner banks

questions.q: Why are deltas fertile and good for agriculture?
questions.a: The river deposits rich alluvial soil there, which supports crops such as rice and jute.
s: Rich alluvial soil deposited by the river
Supports crops such as rice and jute

questions.q: The Sundarbans is an example of a
questions.a: delta

questions.q: Deltas support crops such as rice and ____.
questions.a: jute

questions.q: The Grand Anicut (Kallanai) in Tamil Nadu is an example of using a river for
questions.a: irrigation

questions.q: Give two ways in which waterfalls are useful to humans.
questions.a: They attract tourists and support local tourism and economy, and the force of falling water can be used to generate hydroelectric power.

questions.q: Why are deltas densely settled although they are prone to flooding?
questions.a: Deltas have fertile alluvial soil, support fishing and are centres of trade and transport on navigable rivers. But their low land makes flooding a risk.
s: Gives reasons for settlement such as fertile soil or trade

questions.q: Describe the landforms of the upper, middle and lower course of a river.
questions.a: Upper course: V-shaped valleys, waterfalls and rapids from steep gradients and strong erosion. Middle course: meanders, oxbow lakes and floodplains as the river loses energy and deposits sediment. Lower course: deltas, levees and alluvial fans from heavy deposition.

questions.q: A fan-shaped or triangular area of land at a river mouth is a
questions.a: delta

questions.q: Why are the banks of a meander good for farming and settlement?
questions.a: Fertile soil is deposited along the banks, supporting agriculture, and the gentle slopes near meanders are suitable for villages and towns.

questions.q: Explain how a waterfall forms.
questions.a: In the upper course a river flows over rocks of different hardness. Hard rock resists erosion while the softer rock below is worn away. This creates a steep vertical drop over which the river falls.
s: Softer rock below is worn away
Creates a steep drop in the upper course

questions.q: Tara says deltas are formed by river erosion. Evaluate.
questions.a: She is wrong. Deltas are formed by deposition of the sediments the river has carried from upstream.

questions.q: Describe how you would draw and label a delta.
questions.a: Draw a river flowing into a sea, splitting into several channels called distributaries with islands or bars of deposited sediment between them, forming a fan or triangle at the sea, and label the river, distributaries, islands and sea.
s: River and distributaries drawn and labelled

concepts.name: Landforms of waves, glaciers, wind and underground water
concepts.description: Landforms made by coastal waves, glaciers, wind and underground water, and how humans use them.
concepts.idea: Each agent of gradation creates its own landforms by eroding and depositing.
concepts.rule: Coast: beaches, sand bars, cliffs, wave-cut platforms, caves, arches, stacks. Glaciers: U-shaped valleys, cirques, aretes, hanging valleys, fjords, moraines. Wind: yardangs, ventifacts, deflation hollows, desert pavements, dunes. Underground water: caves, stalactites, stalagmites, sinkholes, karst.
concepts.example: A sea arch collapses to leave a sea stack.

questions.q: A beach is formed by
questions.a: deposition of sediments by waves

questions.q: Moraines are formed by
questions.a: deposition of rocks, soil and debris (till) by glaciers
o: deposition of rocks, soil and debris (till) by glaciers

questions.q: Stalactites hang from the ceiling of a cave and stalagmites rise from the ____.
questions.a: floor

questions.q: U-shaped valleys are carved by
questions.a: glaciers

questions.q: Which are landforms of coastal erosion?
questions.a: cliffs, wave-cut platforms, caves, arches and stacks
o: cliffs, wave-cut platforms, caves, arches and stacks

questions.q: Which are landforms of glacial erosion?
questions.a: cirques, aretes, hanging valleys and fjords
o: cirques, aretes, hanging valleys and fjords

questions.q: Which are landforms made by wind erosion?
questions.a: yardangs, ventifacts, deflation hollows and desert pavements
o: yardangs, ventifacts, deflation hollows and desert pavements

questions.q: Barchan dunes are
questions.a: crescent-shaped and form where sand is limited and wind blows from one direction
o: crescent-shaped and form where sand is limited and wind blows from one direction
star-shaped and form where winds come from many directions
long ridges made only by rivers

questions.q: Explain how a sea cave, an arch and a stack are related.
questions.a: Waves erode weak parts of a headland to form caves. When caves on opposite sides meet they form an arch. When the arch collapses, an isolated pillar of rock, a stack, is left.
s: Caves form by wave erosion, and become an arch

questions.q: A fjord is
questions.a: a deep narrow inlet formed when the sea floods a glacial valley
o: a deep narrow inlet formed when the sea floods a glacial valley
a sand ridge in a desert

questions.q: Sinkholes are also called ____.
questions.a: dolines

questions.q: Star dunes form where
questions.a: winds come from different directions
o: wind blows from one direction only

questions.q: Name the three types of moraines and say where each forms.
questions.a: Lateral moraines form along the sides of a glacier, terminal moraines at its end, marking its furthest advance, and medial moraines where two glaciers meet and their lateral moraines join in the middle.

questions.q: How are beaches useful to humans?
questions.a: They are tourist destinations that boost the local economy, provide fishing areas and act as natural barriers against strong waves and coastal erosion.

questions.q: Name landforms made by (i) sea waves, (ii) glaciers, (iii) wind and (iv) underground water, giving two for each.
questions.a: (i) Cliffs and stacks. (ii) Cirques and fjords. (iii) Yardangs and dunes. (iv) Caves and sinkholes (or stalactites and stalagmites).

questions.q: Sinkholes and caves are produced by
questions.a: underground water acting on soluble rocks like limestone
o: underground water acting on soluble rocks like limestone

questions.q: Why are glaciers important to humans?
questions.a: They are crucial sources of fresh water, feeding rivers that sustain people downstream, and their landforms provide tourism and sometimes fertile soil and harbours.
s: Another benefit such as tourism or fertile soil

questions.q: Explain how sand dunes benefit humans.
questions.a: Dunes act as natural barriers against desertification and wind erosion, protect coastal settlements from strong winds and waves, provide areas for tourism and adventure sports, and give sand for construction.
s: Barrier against wind erosion or desertification

questions.q: Ali says all landforms are made by rivers. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. Waves, glaciers, wind and underground water also create landforms, such as beaches, U-shaped valleys, dunes and caves.

questions.q: Make a chart of five landforms, the agent that formed each and one use to humans.
questions.a: Delta: river deposition, fertile farmland. Beach: waves, tourism. Fjord: glacier, harbour. Dune: wind, barrier against wind erosion. Cave: underground water, fresh water or tourism.
s: Correct pairing of agents and landforms

concepts.name: Landforms and disasters: landslides, avalanches, GLOFs and dust storms
concepts.description: The causes of four landform-related disasters and how human activity and climate increase the risk.
concepts.idea: Natural conditions and human activities together make slopes, snow, glacial lakes and dry soil unstable.
concepts.rule: Landslides: heavy rain, earthquakes, steep slopes, deforestation, mining, road construction. Avalanches: heavy snowfall, temperature rise, wind, vibrations, skiing and construction. GLOFs: glacier melt fills lakes and dams of ice or moraine fail. Dust storms: strong winds lift loose dry soil in dry areas.
concepts.example: In February 2021 a sudden flood struck Chamoli district in Uttarakhand.

questions.q: Four disasters associated with landforms in this chapter are
questions.a: landslides, avalanches, GLOFs and dust storms
o: landslides, avalanches, GLOFs and dust storms

questions.q: GLOF stands for
questions.a: Glacial Lake Outburst Flood

questions.q: The sudden instability of snow on steep mountain slopes causes an ____.
questions.a: avalanche

questions.q: In February 2021 a devastating flood struck
questions.a: Chamoli district in Uttarakhand

questions.q: A natural cause of landslides is
questions.a: heavy and continuous rainfall

questions.q: Which human activities can cause landslides?
questions.a: Deforestation, mining, road construction and unplanned hillside construction
o: Deforestation, mining, road construction and unplanned hillside construction

questions.q: Dust storms are common in
questions.a: desert and semi-arid regions

questions.q: A GLOF happens when
questions.a: the natural dam of a glacial lake made of ice or loose moraine collapses
o: the natural dam of a glacial lake made of ice or loose moraine collapses
a volcano erupts on a plain

questions.q: How does heavy rainfall cause landslides?
questions.a: Water seeps into the soil and rocks, increasing their weight and reducing friction, so the slope becomes unstable and can fail.
s: Water seeps in and adds weight
Reduces friction so the slope fails

questions.q: An avalanche can be triggered by
questions.a: heavy snowfall in a short period
o: heavy snowfall in a short period

questions.q: Dust storms lift large amounts of loose, dry soil and ____ into the air.
questions.a: sand

questions.q: Which human activities can trigger avalanches?
questions.a: skiing, trekking or construction on snowy mountain slopes
o: skiing, trekking or construction on snowy mountain slopes

questions.q: Name two factors that increase dust storms.
questions.a: Prolonged drought and low rainfall, sparse vegetation cover from deforestation, overgrazing or poor farming, and climate change with extreme weather.

questions.q: Give two causes of Glacial Lake Outburst Floods.
questions.a: Rapid melting of glaciers because of rising temperatures raises the lake level; heavy rain or snowfall adds water; earthquakes, avalanches or landslides can weaken or strike the dam.

questions.q: List natural and human factors that raise the risk of landslides on a hillside, and say how each acts.
questions.a: Natural: heavy rain adds water weight, earthquakes shake the slope, steep slopes and loose rocks. Human: deforestation removes roots that hold soil, mining and road construction disturb the slope, poor drainage lets water build up.
s: How they make the slope unstable

questions.q: The disaster linked to glaciers and high mountain lakes is
questions.a: a GLOF

questions.q: How can earthquakes and volcanic eruptions lead to landslides?
questions.a: They shake the ground and weaken slopes, which can trigger landslides.

questions.q: Prepare a mitigation plan for landslides in a hill town.
questions.a: Avoid unplanned construction on steep slopes, improve drainage to remove excess water, plant trees and keep vegetation, control mining and road cutting, and set up warnings and safe evacuation routes.

questions.q: Riya says landslides happen only because of nature. Evaluate.
questions.a: She is wrong. Natural factors like rain and earthquakes matter, but human activities such as deforestation, mining and unplanned construction also make slopes unstable.

questions.q: Write a short safety message for a poster on avalanches or landslides in your own words.
questions.a: For example: "Avoid building or cutting slopes on steep hillsides; keep drains clear; plant trees; and move to safe ground when you see cracks or hear rumbling."
